parties:
Tahurul Karim @ Tahurul Karim Khan Chowdhury  ------- Petitioner.
Vs.
Abdul Hashim and others  ------- Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
Ranadhir Sen J.- These two Rules are directed against an analogous judgment of reversal arising out of two separate proceedings initiated by two different pre-emptors under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act hereinafter referred to as the Act. 

 "A proceeding for pre-emption, in our opinion, cannot be treated on the same level as a suit for partition. It is not correct to say that when a particular piece of land or share thereof is transferred, a right of pre-emption arises, against all the co-sharers or contiguous owners, as the case may be. It may have accrued in favor of all the co-sharers of the seller of the land, as the case may be, but arises only against the purchaser. Ordinarily, there is no question of improper constitution of a preemption proceeding on account of the absence of the non-pre-empting co-sharers or contiguous owners. In a proceeding for pre-emption under section 26E of the Bengal Tenancy Act or section 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, under which only the co-sharers have the right of pre-emption, it is not necessary to join all the co-sharers in such a proceeding for pre-emption. There is nothing inherently defective in the constitution of such a proceeding in the absence of the remaining co-sharers but the Legislature, in order to avoid multiplicity of the litigation, has provided in sub-section (2) of section 96, that in addition to the transferee, the co-sharer tenants of the holding as well as the holders of the contiguous lands shall be made parties and sub-section (4) of the said section provided that such co-sharer tenants or holders of contiguous lands shall have to apply within the period referred to in sub-section. (1) i.e., 4 months of the date of knowledge, or within 2 months of the date of the service of notice of application, whichever is earlier, and such of the persons as have not applied either under sub-section (1) or under the said sub-section shall not have any further right to purchase under section 96. This provision appears to have been enacted by the Legislature for the benefit of persons seeking for pre-emption so that they may not be harassed by multiplicity of litigations in future. It does not appear from a perusal of the provision of section 96 that it was the intent of the Legislature that the penalty for non-impleading a person as contemplated in sub-section (2) is the invalidity of the order which may be ultimately made in the said proceeding. The question whether a person is a necessary party under sub-section (2) is a question of fact and the object of this provision seems to provide the co-sharer tenants and the holders of contiguous lands with the opportunity of availing themselves of the provision of the said sub-section. Since the benefit conferred under the said provision is meant for certain individuals, they can very well be waived. In that view of the matter the positive injunction contained in the said sub-section as to the making of parties in spite of its being couched in mandatory language, should be read as directory." 

 12. The decision relied on by the learned Advocate is of no assistance to him for the proposition he seeks to establish. It cannot be said that section 96(4) is the only remedy available to a person having a subsisting right of pre-emption during the pendency of a previously instituted proceeding under section 96(1). The language of the statute clearly indicates that he has a two-fold remedy. The right of pre-emption may be exercised by a person authorized under the statute either under section96(1) if he had independent knowledge of the transfer or under section 96(4) if notice under section 96(3) (b) of the Act provides him with the knowledge of the transfer for the first time. This is deducible from the two-fold period of limitation prescribed under the two provisions. Section 96(1) provides for a period of limitation of 4 months from the date of service of notice under section 89 or within 4 months from the date of the knowledge of transfer in respect of a person who claims to be a co-sharer; for a person claiming pre-emption as a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred, the period of limitation is 4 months from the date of the knowledge of such transfer. Sub-section (4) of section 96 enable the remaining co-sharer tenants including transferees to join in a pending application under sub-section (1) of section 96 within the period referred to in sub-section (1) or within two months from the date of service of notice under section 96(3)(b)whichever in earlier. The two-fold remedy refers to the two different sources of the knowledge of the transfer and the consequent two different periods of limitation otherwise the expression "whichever is earlier" becomes superfluous. It is, therefore, evident that this is an enabling provision and does not operate as a bar to an independent proceeding under section 96(1) of the Act. Reference may be made to the case of Jamiyat Ali vs. Mrs. Cheman Ara Begum 20 DLR 480 where an independent application under section 96(1) was found to be a valid application although it was filed during the pendency of another application for pre-emption, A similar view was taken by Mukherjee, J. in the case of Jahiruddin Cain & others vs. Mohammad Shoukat Ali Biswas & others 52 C.W.N. 95. This case was under section 26F of Bengal Tenancy Act. It has been held in this case that a co-sharer tenant is entitled to maintain an independent application for preemption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act even though an application under that section has been previously made by another co-sharer tenant. Joining in the application under section 26F (4) is not the only remedy which a co-sharer tenant can pursue. 

 13. The learned Judge construed sub-section (4) of section 26F which is almost similar to Section 96(4) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, in the following terms: "A glance at the language of Sub-section (4) would convince anybody that the provision embodied therein is merely permissive, and the last lines of the paragraph make it perfectly clear that a co-sharer had a two-fold remedy open to him namely, either to make an independent application under sub-sec.(1) of Sec. 26F, or to join in an application already made by another co-sharer as provided for in sub-sec.(4). "In the instant case, the application under section 96(1) of the Act at the instance of Tahurul Karim Khan Chowdhury was pending on the date of the independent application under Section 96(1) was filed by Abdul Hashim. This application was filed within four months from the date of the transfer. Abdul Hashim claims to have derived the knowledge of the transfer from the transfer itself and not from the alleged service of notice of Misc. case No. 4 of 1969. In para 5 of his application he made a clear statement that such proceeding in pending. It need not be re-stated that a right of pre-emption accrues on transfer. The pre-emptor in Misc. case No. 61 of 1969 disclosed his knowledge of the transfer independent of the pendency of Misc. case No. 4 of 1969. It, therefore, necessarily follows that Abdul Has him did not derive the knowledge of the transfer on the basis of any notice allegedly served under Section 96(3) (b) of the Act. Since Abdul Hashim had an earlier and independent knowledge of transfer, he was not required under section 96(4) of the Act to join in the application under section 96(1) of the Act already pending at the instance of Tahurul Karim Khan Chowdhury. In this view of the matter it may be observed that Section 96(4) of the Act does not control a right of preemption arising under section 96(1) of the Act in favor of a preemption who has an independent and prior knowledge of the transfer and an independent application filed within four months of the knowledge of the transfer is competent and valid within the meaning and scope of section 96.
